rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The Fight Goes On
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a small band of cheerful friends camped in a green hollow at the foot of a high hill, a cook fire and little tents under a starry sky, a huge golden wicker castle with twisted towers glowing faintly above them, a girl in a blue dress hugging a gold dishpan, calm night light, cozy storybook illustration

blocks.text: The fight at the wicker castle went on all afternoon, and the golden towers flashed strangely in the sun. Ugu the Shoemaker shot sparks and spells from his high windows, and the great wicker walls creaked and bent under the Wizard's best magic — but they would not fall.

"Fall, please," muttered the Wizard, waving both hands. The walls only creaked. The Cowardly Lion gave his biggest roar, which shook the twisted towers, and even the Frogman's grandest speech only made the walls hum.

At last the Wizard raised his hand for stillness. "We cannot take the castle today," he said, "and a wise magician knows when to stop. Tomorrow we shall be cleverer. We shall camp at the foot of the hill, rest well, and learn more first."
The friends make camp in a green hollow below the wicker castle.

So they camped in a green hollow where the grass was soft and the little stream was sweet. Cayke kept her golden dishpan safe under her arm, for it was the treasure this whole journey had begun with. The Sawhorse dozed standing up, as wooden horses do.
Ask your child: the friends stop fighting for the night, even though they are worried. Why is resting part of being brave? What helps you steady yourself when something is hard?

In the night, Dorothy woke and saw a light moving behind the highest window of the castle. Somebody up there was awake, walking up and down, up and down. "The shoemaker is worried too," said the Wizard softly, when she told him. "That is a good sign. Worried people make mistakes." And he tucked his hat over his eyes and went back to sleep.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · More Friends Come
chapters.artPrompt: a little girl and an old sailor with a wooden leg and a quiet boy walking over green hills toward a band of waiting friends, a sleek glass cat with pink brains trotting ahead with tail up, morning sunshine, cheerful hopeful storybook illustration

blocks.text: In the morning a shout came from the ridge, and over the green hills marched more friends, hurrying to help: little Trot, Button-Bright with his hands in his pockets, old Cap'n Bill with his wooden leg, and the Glass Cat walking daintily between them with her tail in the air.

"We heard the Princess was lost," said Trot, "so we came as fast as anything could carry us." She had a fishhook in her hat and stories in her pocket. Button-Bright said nothing at all, which was his way, but he had brought his sharpest thinking face. Cap'n Bill touched his sailor cap to the company.

The Glass Cat sat down before the wicker castle, gazed up at it with her diamond eyes, and wrinkled her pink nose. "Anyone can see his treasures are kept at the top," she said. "Cats know houses. It is a pity cats cannot vote."
Trot, Button-Bright, Cap'n Bill and the Glass Cat arrive to help.
New word: reinforce — to make stronger by adding more. Every new friend reinforced the little company. When did one more helper make a hard job easier for you?

The Wizard was glad of them, for the company was small and the castle was large, and a wizard always plans before he battles. "First we must find where Ozma is hidden," he said. "The castle is big, Ugu is sly, and guessing wastes time. We need a helper who cannot tell a lie."

"Someone who cannot tell a lie," said the Wizard slowly — and then he clapped his hands. "I know just the one: the Little Pink Bear of Bear Center, whose every answer is true. We shall start for Bear Center this very morning."

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · The Little Pink Bear
chapters.artPrompt: a smiling lavender plush bear king with a jeweled crown sitting on a velvet throne beside a tiny solemn pink bear, a company of travelers gathered respectfully in a cozy lamplit bear house, acorn cups on a little table, warm golden light, gentle storybook illustration

blocks.text: A pleasant day's journey beyond the hills lay a cozy country called Bear Center, where the King of the Teddy Bears lived in a house of velvet and gold. He was the Lavender Bear King, soft and smiling, with a jeweled crown upon his head, and the whole court of little bears bowed to the travelers.

The whole company was welcomed graciously, and berry juice was served in little acorn cups. "And what do you wish to know?" asked the Bear King. "For my Little Pink Bear answers every question, and everything he says is true."

The Little Pink Bear was small and pink and very solemn. The Wizard asked the first question. "Is Princess Ozma of Oz safe and alive?" The Little Pink Bear answered in his small, truthful voice: "Yes." And everyone drew a long, long breath.
The Little Pink Bear answers their questions, and every answer is true.

"Is she in the wicker castle?" asked Dorothy. "Yes," said the Pink Bear. "Can we open the door where she sleeps?" asked the Wizard. "Not until the shoemaker's stolen magic is taken from him," said the Pink Bear. Then he sat up very straight, for his evening's work was done.
Ask your child: the Little Pink Bear always tells the truth, even when the truth is hard. Why do the friends trust him completely? Talk about why honest answers make plans go right.

"Then take my Pink Bear with you," said the Lavender Bear King, wrapping him in a warm scarf. "His answers never fail, and neither, I think, will you." And the company set off back toward the wicker castle with much lighter hearts than they had come.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · The Giantess of the Valley
chapters.artPrompt: a towering friendly-but-tricky giantess in a patched gown leaning down to smile at a small band of travelers in the doorway of a vast odd castle in a deep green valley, strange transformed creatures peeking from the halls, tall cliffs above, slightly funny not scary, whimsical storybook illustration

blocks.text: On the way back, the path led through a deep green valley where a castle stood as tall as the cliffs. This was the home of Yoop the giantess, a Yookoohoo magician taller than any tree, who loved changing things into other things just for fun.

"Visitors!" she boomed, looking delighted. "How nice. Do come in and stay forever." The great door closed behind them with a boom, and she smiled down at her guests the way a cat smiles at a cream pot. It was not a comforting smile.

Her halls were full of odd creatures that had once been something else, for the giantess transformed things whenever she felt bored — and she was very often bored. The friends kept close together and spoke in polite whispers.
The giantess Yoop welcomes the travelers into her strange valley castle.

New word: transform — to change one thing into another. The giantess transforms things just for fun. Ask your child: is it fun for the thing that gets transformed? What would you never want to be changed into?

Then the Frogman rose to the occasion, as he always did. He made the grandest speech of his life, about liberty and cookies and the ancient rights of travelers. The giantess laughed until her towers shook. "Very well," she said, wiping her eyes. "One honest answer, and then you may go."

"Ugu's strength is his stolen bag of magic tools," she said. "Take that away from him, and his spells will crumble like stale bread. Now shoo, all of you, before I change my mind — and my guests." And she opened the great door, and the friends did not walk out; they RAN.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Shoemaker's Shapes
chapters.artPrompt: a great shape-shifting shadow of bear wings and serpent coils swirling over a golden wicker castle while a brave cowardless lion roars in front of a small band of friends on the hillside below, sparks in the sky, dramatic but not frightening, vivid storybook illustration

blocks.text: Back at the wicker castle, the Wizard gathered everyone close. "The giantess says his power sits in my stolen bag of tools," he said. "So, while Ugu is busy changing shapes, one of us must be quick and small and silent." Everyone looked at the Glass Cat. "Naturally," said the Glass Cat.

The next morning the battle began again. The Wizard threw bright sparks at the towers, and Ugu came out furious. He changed himself into a great growly bear, then a hissing serpent, then a bird with wings as wide as sails — one frightening shape after another, bigger and stranger each time.

The Cowardly Lion stood in front of all his friends and roared, louder than he had ever roared in his life. And for once, just for once, he was not thinking about being afraid at all. The monstrous shapes flinched and drew back.
Ugu changes into one frightening shape after another, and the Lion roars.
Ask your child: the Cowardly Lion is afraid almost all the time — but today he roars first. What does that tell you about courage? Does being brave mean feeling no fear at all?

Ugu grew tired of changing. His spells came slower and slower, and his monstrous shape flickered like a candle in the wind. High in the topmost window, among all the stolen treasures, the black bag of magic tools sat waiting on a table.

"Now!" whispered the Wizard. The Glass Cat poured herself through a gap in the wicker wall like a ribbon of silver, and was gone inside, without a sound. Dorothy held the Lion's paw, and the Frogman held his breath.

chapters.title: Chapter 10 · The Black Bag
chapters.artPrompt: a sleek glass cat with pink brains dragging a fat black bag down golden wicker stairs by its handle, shelves of mismatched stolen treasures behind her, an angry shape-shifting magician lunging outside, action and sparkle, exciting storybook illustration

blocks.text: Inside the castle, the Glass Cat padded along the golden wicker halls, past shelves of stolen cups and clocks and crowns and kettles. Everything in them had been taken from somebody, which was why nothing matched. At the very top, fat and dusty, sat the black bag of magic tools.

She caught the handle in her teeth. The bag was heavy, but cats find a way, and it served the thief right. She dragged it bumping down every stair, screech by screech, and the whole strange castle seemed to shake with the noise.

Ugu heard it and spun round in his monster shape. "THIEF!" he bellowed — which was funny, coming from him. He lunged for the cat, and outside the friends shouted and waved their hats, to keep his eyes looking outward instead of in.
The Glass Cat drags the stolen bag of tools down the wicker stairs.
New word: distract — to pull someone's attention away for a moment. The friends distracted Ugu so the Glass Cat could work. When can a good distraction be the kindest and cleverest plan?

The Glass Cat shot out through the bars with the bag, and the Wizard caught it and hugged it like a long-lost kitten. "My old tools!" he said happily. "Now, Ugu the Shoemaker — let us see you practice magic without your stolen kit!"

Up on his high balcony, Ugu stood perfectly still, breathing hard. His spells sputtered and died like wet matches, for his borrowed power was gone. He looked down at his own two empty hands. Then he raised both arms for one last, enormous spell — much too enormous, as everyone was about to see.

chapters.title: Chapter 11 · A Small Grey Dove
chapters.artPrompt: a small grey dove perched on a tiny hidden door behind a wicker curtain, a princess waking gently on a little white bed in a beam of morning sun, a girl and a kindly wizard and friends crowding happily at the doorway, soft golden light, tender hopeful storybook illustration

blocks.text: Ugu's last spell was far bigger than his empty hands could hold. It burst over the hilltop in a whirl of purple smoke — and when the smoke cleared away, a small grey dove stood on the balcony, blinking in the sunshine and very surprised at himself.

The dove ruffled his feathers. Then, to everyone's astonishment, he began to coo — softly, comfortably, as if a great weight had rolled off him at last. As a dove he owned nothing and needed nothing, and somehow that felt exactly like freedom.
Behind the secret door, the friends find Princess Ozma safe asleep.

"Now show us, if you please, where the Princess sleeps," said the Wizard kindly. The dove fluttered along a corridor and perched on a small door hidden behind a wicker curtain. Cayke pulled it open with trembling hands, and everyone crowded close behind her.

There, on a little white bed, lay Princess Ozma of Oz, fast asleep in a beam of morning sun. The Wizard whispered the waking charm he knew best, and Ozma opened her eyes and smiled. "I had the strangest dream," she said. "But it is over, and you are all here."
Ask your child: the dove schemed and stole for years, then gave it all up in one morning. What do you think freedom felt like to him? Talk about a time when letting go felt good.

They led Ozma out into the sunshine, and the Great Book of Records, the Magic Picture and the black bag were packed up carefully for home. And the little grey dove followed them all the way down the hill, cooing a small, contented song.

chapters.title: Chapter 12 · The Grand Homecoming
chapters.artPrompt: a joyful feast in a grand emerald palace hall with long tables of cakes and cookies, a fairy princess smiling at a crowd of happy friends including a lion, a frog gentleman, a cookie cook and a glass cat, a small grey dove on a window sill, sparkling celebration light, warm festive storybook illustration

blocks.text: Back in the Emerald City the palace bells rang and rang. The Magic Picture was hung on its wall, the Great Book of Records opened itself to a clean new page, and the black bag went back into the Wizard's closet, exactly where it belonged.

Cayke baked cookies for everyone in the royal kitchen, and her golden dishpan sat on the shelf where she could watch it shine. At the feast the Frogman stood up to make a speech. "I have a confession," he announced grandly. "I am not really wise. I only look wise." Everyone laughed kindly, for honest frogs are rarer than wise ones.
The Emerald City feasts to welcome Princess Ozma home.

"You looked for me across all of Oz," said Ozma, "with lions and frogs and bears and cats and cookies and one very honest glass cat. I am the luckiest princess in any fairyland." And everybody cheered until the crystal lamps swung and sparkled.

The little grey dove made his home in the palace garden, where the fountains sparkle and the roses climb. Nobody ever shooed him, and nobody ever asked him for anything at all, and he seemed to like that best of all the things in the world.
Ask your child: the dove gave back nothing in the end — but he stopped wanting to take. What is something that made you happy to share instead of keep?

And that night the Emerald City glowed like a jewel box, and every friend was safe at home, and the only thing anybody stole that day was one more cookie from Cayke's tray — which Cayke said they were all very welcome to.
